       1             SENATOR MAZIARZ:  Good morning, everyone.

       2             If I could call this hearing to order,

       3      I, first of all, want to state for the record that

       4      today is Monday, September the 30th, at

       5      approximately 10:15 p.m. [sic].

       6             We are starting a meeting of the

       7      Senate Energy Committee, a public hearing on the

       8      Indian Point contingency plan.

       9             For all those who are present, I want to

      10      thank you all for your attendance.

      11             Apologize probably for the long line -- long,

      12      hot line that you had to wait in to get through

      13      security to get into this building.

      14             I appreciate your patience, as do my

      15      colleagues.

      16             I'm joined today by Senator Patricia Ritchie

      17      from the North Country.

      18             I do want to say, just again for the record,

      19      that we have had responses of members of the Senate

      20      and this Committee who will attend.

      21             Those of you who are familiar with these

      22      hearings know that members do come and go based on

      23      their own time considerations.

      24             I certainly appreciate all of their

      25      attention.





 

                                                                  5
       1             We will be joined shortly by

       2      Senator David Carlucci; Senator Eric Adams, who is,

       3      I think, soon to be Brooklyn Borough President

       4      Eric Adams; Senator Felder, and Senator Dilan, have

       5      all RSVP'd that They will come for at least a part

       6      of this hearing.

       7             We are here today to examine and analyze the

       8      proceeding currently before the Public Service

       9      Commission to examine contingencies in the event,

      10      "in the event," of the closure of Indian Point

      11      Energy Center.

      12             There are currently proceedings before, not

      13      just the Public Service Commission, also before the

      14      Department of Environmental Conservation, and also

      15      before the federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

      16             Of most concern to this Committee is:

      17             The contingency plan, how much that would

      18      cost.

      19             It's been estimated to cost almost, "almost,"

      20      $1 billion to close Indian Point;

      21             Where the power would come from to replace

      22      the current power that is produced by Indian Point;

      23             And where the revenue would be derived from

      24      to pay for those costs.

      25             And I can tell you, myself, and speaking on





 

                                                                  6
       1      behalf of the members, at least the upstate members,

       2      Senator Ritchie and myself of this Committee, and

       3      the other upstate members of the Senate, we

       4      certainly do not want to see those costs, that

       5      burden -- that financial burden, placed upon

       6      businesses and residents outside of the Indian Point

       7      service area, and most particularly, those in

       8      Upstate New York.

       9             I have personally visited the Indian Point

      10      facility.

      11             I have seen how safe that particular facility

      12      is, both from the standpoint of natural disasters,

      13      and manmade disasters, terrorist attacks, and so

      14      forth.

      15             As I said, we are most concerned, "most

      16      concerned," with maintaining a clean, positive

      17      operating facility, and what should happen if these

      18      various agencies determine that something other than

      19      what's currently being done would replace

      20      Indian Point nuclear plant.

      21             So with that, I do want to thank my colleague

      22      Senator Ritchie.

      23             She traveled a great distance to be here

      24      today.

      25             She has been an extremely good partner on the





 

                                                                  7
       1      Energy Committee in going forth.

       2             And, certainly, I've heard from her, in my

       3      opinion, almost far too often, about protecting --

       4      protecting the area of the state that she represents

       5      from any increased costs in energy facilities.

       6             Senator Ritchie, would you like to -- care to

       7      make any opening statement before we go to our first

       8      witnesses?

       9             SENATOR RITCHIE:  Sure.

      10             I would just like to thank Senator Maziarz

      11      for calling this hearing on Indian Point.

      12             This issue is extremely important to me, as

      13      I represent the district that Nine Mile 1 and 2 in

      14      Fitzpatrick are located.

      15             They generate a third of the electricity

      16      upstate.

      17             They actually -- they actually have over a

      18      thousand employees, and are very important, not only

      19      to the rate that people pay in New York State, but

      20      also important to the economy of my district.

      22      today, and appreciate the opportunity to ask some

      23      critically important questions I think that may not,

       1      plants that are in my district.

       3      Senator.

       4             Our first witnesses, and we appreciate very

       5      much them taking the time to be here today:

       6             Is Gil Quinones, the president and CEO of the

       7      New York State Power Authority.

       8             Thank you very much, Gil;

       9             And, also, Rajendra Addepalli, the deputy

      10      director of the Office of Electric, Gas & Water for

      11      the New York State Department of Public Service.

      12             They're going to be testifying together.

      13             I assume, Mr. Quinones, you're going to go

      14      first.

      15             Thank you very much, Rajendra, for being

      16      here.

      17             Oh, I'm sorry.

      18             GIL QUINONES:  It's actually the opposite.

      19             SENATOR MAZIARZ:  The opposite, okay.

      21             GIL QUINONES:  I yield my time to him.

      24             RAJENDRA ADDEPALLI:  Good morning.

      25             Good morning, Senator Maziarz and





 

                                                                  9
       1      Senator Ritchie.

       2             Thank you for giving us the opportunity to

       3      come and discuss these issues with you this morning.

       4             What I will do in my testimony is answer a

       5      few questions, some of which that you have raised

       6      this morning:

       7             Why are we doing this contingency plan?

       8             What is in this plan?

       9             And, what is the cost of this plan?

      10             And, who's going to pay for it?

      11             And, how does it comport with the competitive

      12      wholesale markets that are in place?

      13             So, starting with, "Why do this plan,

      14      contingency plan?" numerous entities have done

      15      reliability analysis in the state, including the

      16      New York ISO and the City of New York, Con Edison,

      17      and others.

      18             And as part of the analysis, they examined

      19      what the reliability ramifications would be if

      20      Indian Point were not available post 2015 December.

      21             And they've all identified that, in summer

      22      2016, there will be reliability violations, and, so,

      23      there's a need to address that concern.

      24             And so how do we, address in, general

      25      retirements of plants in New York State?





 

                                                                  10
       1             Over the last number of years, numerous

       2      plants have retired, thousands of megawatts.

       3             We do have at the commission a policy

       4      statement for retirement of generation units.

       5             The policy statement asked the generators,

       6      about 80 megawatts, to file their notice six months

       7      in advance if the plant were to retire or mothball.

       8             And once a notice is filed, the commission

       9      conducts an analysis of the ramifications of the

      10      plant shutdown, working with the New York

      11      Independent System Operator and with the host

      12      utility (local utility).

      13             If there are no reliability issues, the

      14      plants are allowed to shut down.

      15             But if there are reliability concerns, they

      16      need to be addressed, either by the utilities

      17      through their solutions, such as transmission

      18      upgrades, but sometimes they may take time, in which

      19      case the generator may be asked to stay open through

      20      a commercial arrangement.

      21             The most recent examples -- many -- in the

      22      last number of years, many units have been allowed

      23      to retire because there were no reliability

      24      concerns.

      25             But in two cases recently, there were





 

                                                                  11
       1      concerns, and the utilities said they would need

       2      time to build their transmission solutions, and the

       3      generators were asked to stay open through a

       4      commercial arrangement; namely, for the Dunkirk unit

       5      and for the Cayuga unit.

       6             So, in this case, though, if the unit is not

       7      available post 2015 December, and we only get a

       8      six-month notice, or even a year notice, it's very

       9      difficult to replace the magnitude of the resources

      10      that we are talking about.

      11             There is a lead time needed to replace

      12      through either generation or transmission or demand

      13      reduction.

      14             We have less than three years to go; and, so,

      15      the commission has an obligation to ensure the

      16      reliability is maintained, that the lights stay on.

      17             So it's efficient and effective to have a

      18      plan in place to ensure that the lights stay on.

      19             So, in that context, the commission asked

      20      Con Edison, the primary downstate utility that would

      21      be affected, to work with the Power Authority, and

      22      other parties, like, the Department of Public

      23      Service staff, to come up with a reliability

      24      contingency plan, and Con Edison and NYPA filed one

      25      in February 2013.





 

                                                                  12
       1             So what does the plan consist of?

       2             The plan -- the reliability contingency plan

       3      had three prongs of solutions to address the

       4      reliability needs.

       5             The first prong is the proposed certain

       6      transition projects between Con Edison and the

       7      Power Authority, and one element of New York State

       8      Electric and Gas.

       9             These transmission solutions could be put in

      10      place by 2016 summer, and would address part of the

      11      reliability need.

      12             The second prong was to put in certain

      13      demand-reduction measures that would also help

      14      reduce need, or alleviate the concerns.

      15             The third prong, even after doing these two,

      16      we need more resources to fill the gap, so, they

      17      proposed issuing an RFP (request for proposals) to

      18      get additional incremental new generation or

      19      transmission solutions.

      20             And they asked the commission to approve this

      21      plan.

      22             And the commission, so far, has taken the

      23      following steps:

      24             One, allowed the utilities to move forward

      25      with these three transmission projects, subject to





 

                                                                  13
       1      halting and other conditions, given the lead time

       2      that is needed to implement the plans;

       3             Second, it allowed the RFP to move forward;

       4      to be issued, and get responses;

       5             And, third, it asked Con Edison to work with

       6      the NYSERDA and improve the demand-reduction plan.

       7             So what is in front of the commission right

       8      now is these multitude of solutions that would help

       9      address the reliability need: certain transmission

      10      projects proposed by the utilities, certain demand

      11      reductions proposed by the utilities, and the

      12      responses to the RFP.

      13             The commission asked the department staff to

      14      review the RFP responses, because Con Edison and

      15      NYPA are also in the play with their transmission

      16      projects, for unbiasedness.

      17             The department staff has been reviewing these

      18      proposals, and is expected to find out which is the

      19      optimal portfolio solutions that would meet the

      20      reliability needs, keeping the costs low to

      21      consumers, and addressing the risks that are

      22      entailed in selecting these projects.

      23             So that's the, in essence, contingency plan.

      24             And in terms of what does it cost, clearly,

      25      each of these solutions would lead to certain





 

                                                                  14
       1      investments up front that would be made, whether

       2      it's transmission or demand reduction or a

       3      generation solution.

       4             In addition to satisfying the reliability

       5      need, what these solutions would also provide are

       6      benefits to consumers; economic benefits to

       7      consumers, in terms of reduced energy prices and

       8      reduced capacity prices.

       9             So one has to look at, what is the net cost

      10      to ratepayers of this portfolio of solutions?

      11             Again, our interest is to minimize the cost

      12      to ratepayers, and, to reduce the risks associated

      13      with them.

      14             And, so, the first order of business for us

      15      would be to analyze, What if Indian Point stayed

      16      open, would these solutions still cost ratepayers

      17      money?

      18             But, if the benefits exceed costs, even if

      19      Indian Point stayed open, then it would be in the

      20      interests of the ratepayers to pursue such solutions

      21      that make sense, that not only provide reliability

      22      benefits, but provide economic benefits.

      23             So that analysis is underway in terms of

      24      selecting the optimal portfolio that would

      25      reduce/minimize costs, maximize benefits, and reduce





 

                                                                  15
       1      risks.

       2             In terms of, "How would the costs be

       3      allocated?" the commission asked the department

       4      staff to come up with a straw proposal to address

       5      how to allocate the costs.

       6             The staff star proposal essentially

       7      articulated a so-called "beneficiaries pay

       8      approach," which means, those who would benefit from

       9      these projects should pay for them.

      10             And the benefits were focused on reliability

      11      benefits: who would otherwise be affected, in terms

      12      of reliability, through these projects?

      13             They are the ones benefiting from a

      14      reliability perspective, so they should pay for

      15      these projects.

      16             It's called a "reliability-based

      17      beneficiaries approach."

      18             So that's the straw proposal.

      19             And, we conducted two technical conferences.

      20             We received numerous comments.

      21             There are other entities that have proposed

      22      other approaches, such as, the beneficiaries should

      23      be thought of more broadly.

      24             If there are other benefits beyond pure

      25      reliability benefits, they should be accounted for





 

                                                                  16
       1      in the cost-allocation approach.

       2             So those comments are also being examined.

       3             And, the commission would deal with this

       4      issue, along with the selection of the optimal

       5      portfolios, as to how the costs should be allocated.

       6             And some of the parties have suggested

       7      different approaches for different elements of this

       8      plan.

       9             For example:

      10             Certain demand-reduction measures, costs

      11      should be allocated this way; for certain

      12      generation, it should be done a little bit

      13      differently; and, for transmission, yet differently.

      14             So, they're all being analyzed by us at this

      15      point.

      16             And the next question that comes up is,

      17      Why -- or, how does this comport with the existing

      18      marketplace?

      19             And as I said before, if there is certainty

      20      and there is adequate lead time, it's more than

      21      likely the market would address the needs.

      22             We would not have to intervene in any

      23      fashion.

      24             But given the unique circumstance here, there

      25      is uncertainty, and, given our obligation to keep





 

                                                                  17
       1      the lights on, we have to do this contingency plan.

       2             So what we did to comport with the

       3      marketplace, the first instance of asking for a full

       4      replacement of the power, this is over

       5      2,000 megawatts of a power plant, the reliability

       6      plan that the commission sought is looking at a bare

       7      minimum needed for reliability purposes, just around

       8      1450 megawatts.

       9             So, you're not trying to replace the full

      10      amount, but just to meet the -- enough needed for

      11      reliability purposes.

      12             Second, the RFP that the Power Authority

      13      issued, many elements in the RFP, especially dealing

      14      with the generation, comport with market-price

      15      signals of how efficiently they should be

      16      dispatched.

      17             And, third, many of the -- there are

      18      provisions in the RFP to halt the project.

      19             Should the commission find new information in

      20      the coming months and years that suggests that there

      21      is no need for this project, it could be halted if

      22      it makes sense.

      23             So, in these terms, it is trying to be as

      24      responsive to the needs.

      25             So, in conclusion, it is appropriate, and it





 

                                                                  18
       1      is necessary, for the commission to address this

       2      contingency plan, to meet the reliability needs to

       3      keep the lights on.

       4             And, we are not taking a position as to

       5      whether Indian Point should be open or should shut

       6      down.

       7             That's not our view.

       8             Our view is purely focused on keeping the

       9      lights on.

      10             And, what are the next steps?

      11             We intend to recommend to the commission, in

      12      the very near future, the optimal set of solutions

      13      that would help address the reliability need,

      14      minimizing net cost to ratepayers, reducing the

      15      risk, and also deal with the cost-allocation

      16      recommendation.

      17             That concludes my remarks, and Mr. Quinones

      18      will provide his.

      19             SENATOR MAZIARZ:  Thank you.

      20             GIL QUINONES:  Thank you very much.

      21             Good morning, Senator Maziarz.

      22             Good morning, Senator Ritchie.

      23             Good to be with you here in southeast

      24      New York.

      25             As you know, we meet a lot upstate in your





 

                                                                  19
       1      areas.

       2             My name is Gil Quinones.

       3             I am the president and chief executive

       4      officer of the New York Power Authority.

       5             Thank you for the opportunity to testify

       6      today regarding the nature and importance of

       7      generator-reliability contingency plans.

       8             As I will discuss in more detail, contingency

       9      plans allow for advanced measures to prepare for

      10      large power-plant retirements, such as the potential

      11      closures of the Indian Point Energy Center in

      12      Westchester County or the Dunkirk and Cayuga coal

      13      facilities in Western New York.

      14             Given the uncertainties surrounding the

      15      continued operation of such facilities, and in light

      16      of their size, impact on transmission flows, and

      17      proximity to load centers, such preparations are

      18      critical to the continued resilience and reliability

      19      of this state's interconnected electric system.

      20             In 2012, Governor Cuomo proposed an

      21      Innovative Energy Highway Initiative to upgrade and

      22      modernize the state's power system.

      23             I was privileged to serve as a co-chair of a

      24      task force that the Governor named to oversee

      25      development of a series of recommendations to bring





 

                                                                  20
       1      this far-reaching proposal to fruition.

       2             One of our most significant recommendations

       3      called for the development and implementation of

       4      reliability contingency plans, to prepare for

       5      potential large power-plant retirements.

       6             The task force recognized that recent and

       7      pending environmental regulations, coupled with low

       8      demand growth and low natural gas prices, could lead

       9      to accelerated retirements of older facilities in

      10      the state, creating uncertainty for the power

      11      supply.

      12             The recommended action addressed a critical

      13      aspect of this problem.

      14             By virtue of plant size, location, or issues

      15      regarding the timing of potential retirements, the

      16      electricity market may not be in a position to

      17      respond adequately to the shutdown of certain power

      18      plants once retirement is announced.

      19             This is the potential case with Indian Point,

      20      a nuclear power plant of approximately

      21      2,000 megawatts located in the village of Buchanan,

      22      about 30 miles north of the state's major load

      23      center in New York City and owned by subsidiaries of

      24      Entergy Corporation.

      25             As I have indicated, the need to address





 

                                                                  21
       1      actual or potential power-plant retirements goes

       2      well beyond Indian Point.

       3             In fact, the New York Independent System

       4      Operator recently reported that the owners of 19 of

       5      the state's generating facilities, representing

       6      almost 1700 megawatts of capacity, have either

       7      retired them during the past 17 months or served

       8      notice of their intent to do so in 2013.

       9             Just over a month ago, Entergy itself

      10      announced that it intends to close its 635-megawatt

      11      Vermont Yankee nuclear plant by the end of next

      12      year, essentially, giving the ISO-New England region

      13      only a one-year lead time to prepare for their

      14      retirement.

      15             Nationwide, the retirements of five nuclear

      16      reactors have been announced within the past year.

      17             This is an industry trend that we cannot

      18      ignore.

      19             The Indian Point situation is exacerbated by

      20      the plant's importance to the New York City load

      21      center, and by the fact that the federal license for

      22      one of the two units expired two days ago, and the

      23      other is scheduled to expire in December 2015.

      24             Although Nuclear Regulatory Commission

      25      regulations allow continued operations until the





 

                                                                  22
       1      license-renewal process is complete, significant

       2      uncertainty persists regarding whether Entergy will

       3      be able to obtain all the permits and approvals

       4      required to keep both units operating for an

       5      extended period beyond the expiration of their

       6      licenses.

       7             Thus, in adopting the Energy Highway Task

       8      Force's recommendation, the Public Service

       9      Commission, in a November 30, 2012, order commenced

      10      a proceeding specifically to solicit a reliability

      11      contingency plan for Indian Point.

      12             As you have heard from Mr. Addepalli,

      13      Con Edison and NYPA developed a contingency plan for

      14      Indian Point, and filed it with the commission

      15      earlier this year.

      16             The plan identified 1,450 megawatts of

      17      reliability deficiencies that would occur in the

      18      event Indian Point shuts down.

      19             Part of the plan called for NYPA to issue a

      20      request for proposals to solicit a target

      21      1,350 megawatts in generation and transmission

      22      proposals from private developers, which we did on

      23      April 3rd.

      24             As Mr. Addepalli indicated, DPS

      25      (Department of Public Service) staff is now





 

                                                                  23
       1      evaluating responses to the RFP.

       2             I would now like to address two issues that

       3      have been raised in public statements related to

       4      this hearing.

       5             First, contrary to what has been alleged, no

       6      Power Authority revenue from any source, including

       7      the Niagara Power Project or the St. Lawrence FDR

       8      project, will be used to subsidize projects arising

       9      from the RFP.

      10             Second, NYPA has no role in determining

      11      whether Indian Point will be retired.

      12             Our involvement in the RFP and

      13      contingency-planning process is intended only to

      14      prepare for a possible shutdown.

      15             The Power Authority, in fact, is unable to

      16      predict whether or when the Indian Point Energy

      17      Center will be retired; yet, it is that very

      18      uncertainty surrounding Indian Point's relicensing

      19      and permitting issues that makes it critically

      20      important to plan ahead to prevent the significant

      21      adverse impacts on the state's electric system that

      22      will occur if suitable replacement power is needed,

      23      and unavailable.

      24             The Indian Point contingency plan is a

      25      prudent and essential insurance policy for the





 

                                                                  24
       1      state's citizens.

       2             It will provide us with the best possible

       3      combination of reliable, economical, and

       4      environmentally compatible power sources.

       5             In contrast, the failure to act now in timely

       6      fashion would represent a striking abdication of the

       7      state's responsibilities and would violate the most

       8      basics standards of effective public policy.

       9             This concludes my prepared remarks, and

      10      Mr. Addepalli and I will be pleased to take your

      11      questions.

      13      Mr. Addepalli and Mr. Quinones.

      14             We appreciate, again, you being here today.

      16      graphics up here.

      18             Oh, okay.

      19             Gil, this document is from NYPA's Prosperous
